subject: zcode-rcos: the deterministic eligibility engine (GPT round-6 ruling, step 4). A standalone pure policy engine that answers whether a named capability is PERMITTED to compete or execute in a supplied context, writes that answer as a write-once decision artifact, and is consumed — never recreated — by the invocation kernel.

spec.ruling_verbatim: extract the current mode ladder from the kernel, make eligibility a standalone pure policy engine with its own immutable decision artifact, and make the invocation kernel consume—not recreate—that decision. Step 4 ends there.
spec.invariant: Eligibility decides whether a named capability is permitted to compete or execute in the supplied context. It never decides which capability is best. No semantic routing. No scoring. No ranking. No task interpretation.
spec.signature: eligibility(registry_entry, capability_runtime_state, caller_context) -> decision. No mutation, no adapter execution, no model call, no trace write.

verdict_basis: Before this step the mode ladder lived inside the invocation kernel, so 'may this run' and 'make this run' were the same code path and the permission question had no artifact of its own. After it, permission is a pure function over a closed context vocabulary, every applicable reason is reported at once in a canonical order, the answer is a write-once self-verifying artifact, and the kernel refuses to execute without one while keeping its own execution-safety checks. Fifteen of fifteen ship-bar items pass against live evidence; 60/60 tests green; step 4 moved no registry or trace byte, proven by commit range rather than by a single measurement: git diff bab54a7 187a61b -- registry/ traces/ is empty. The registry sha recorded in this receipt is the value at that commit; the live registry has since moved only because an unrelated machine-written study loop added two asserted eval records on top. The one finding that does not flatter the step is left standing rather than papered over: normal-mode eligibility is 0/22 on the real registry, because none of the twenty promoted capabilities declares an adapter or rests on an RCOS-executed eval. Permission is not executability, and the engine is the first thing in this repo that says so out loud.

ship_bar.item: Eligibility is a pure deterministic function.
ship_bar.evidence: 66 evaluations of the real registry across all three purposes. The pure core (orderReasons, executabilityReason, buildContext, isPlainObject, validateContext, decide) was extracted by source and contains zero I/O identifiers — no fs, no child_process, no Date, no Math.random. Repeating an identical evaluation returns byte-identical reasons. deriveRuntimeState is declared impure_by_design and excluded: it is the read-only reader that produces the state the pure core consumes. Canonical ordering was checked against a deliberately shuffled input: the output is a permutation of the input AND equals the rank-sorted order.

ship_bar.item: Zero adapter execution occurs during eligibility.
ship_bar.evidence: The eligibility module contains no process-launch identifiers. The adapter side-effect surface is the invocation work directory: invocations on disk were 7 before the 66 evaluations and 7 after, so no invocation dir was created.

registry/capability-registry.json sha256 identical before and after the entire verification run (which included 66 evaluations and a full npm test): bb4c5fac731f5b84420d3fadc030d23d38b19289c8f1fd4193206f7577d9d259.
All 9 decisions written by the step-4 build carry schema 'rcos-eligibility/1'; zero carry any other schema.

All 13 decisions on disk verify clean under rcos eligibility-verify --decision: the 9 pinned in this commit and the 4 written by this receipt's own CLI dogfood. Write-once was proven in a scratch probe home rather than on a real artifact: re-deciding under an existing decision id is refused with 'eligibility decision elig_20260918T031803Z-93695a already exists — decisions are write-once and never rewritten', and a copy edited after writing is detected with 'decision integrity mismatch — the decision was edited after it was written'. The probe home was removed afterwards.

ship_bar.item: Reason codes are enumerable and deterministic.
ship_bar.evidence: 14 codes, REASON_CODES.length === 14, and REASON_RANK is a total order 0..13 with no gaps or ties. Canonical order: eligible, unknown_capability, retired, candidate_not_allowed, unsupported_adapter, missing_adapter, missing_contract, not_executable, provenance_asserted, latest_eval_blocked, latest_eval_fix, no_ship_eval, eval_stale, forensic_reason_required. The order is the order of the question each reason answers: identity → permission → executability (most specific first, exactly one emitted) → evidence reality → evidence quality (at most one) → context. 'eligible' is rank 0 but is guarded against ever being emitted as a reason.

ship_bar.item: Multiple simultaneous failures are all reported.
ship_bar.evidence: Four live decisions report 3 reasons each, e.g. filmstrip-verify/normal → [not_executable, provenance_asserted, no_ship_eval] and reuse-ledger/normal → [candidate_not_allowed, provenance_asserted, no_ship_eval]. Max reasons observed on a live decision: 3. A caller learns every problem from one decision instead of fixing them one at a time.

ship_bar.item: Kernel no longer contains registry-status/mode eligibility policy.
ship_bar.evidence: The kernel was scanned line by line for the policy vocabulary (candidate_not_allowed, no_ship_eval, provenance_asserted, require_current_ship, allow_candidate, not eligible for normal invocation, eval_fresh): zero occurrences. It was also scanned for status comparisons (cap.status ===, status === '...'): zero occurrences. The kernel imports the eligibility module; it does not reimplement it.

ship_bar.item: Kernel requires a valid eligible decision before execution.
ship_bar.evidence: A naked invocation is refused with 'invocation requires an eligibility decision — construct a caller context and run the eligibility engine first (rcos run and eval-run do this for you), then pass its decision id'. The kernel exports no eligibility function of its own (Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty(invocation, 'eligibility') === false), so a caller cannot reach around the engine through the kernel. The manifest records the decision id and re-hashes the decision bytes; verifyInvocation checks them.

ship_bar.item: Execution-safety checks remain inside the kernel.
ship_bar.evidence: Proven by construction: a capability's decision comes back eligible:true, a control invocation through that same decision reaches 'completed', and then four sabotages each produce a SEALED refusal from the kernel's own checks with adapter_exit_code null — entrypoint deleted → blocked ('adapter entrypoint is missing'), entrypoint chmod 644 → blocked ('adapter entrypoint is not executable'), contract file deleted → blocked ('declared contract is not usable: declared contract is missing'), input the contract refuses → rejected ('input did not satisfy the declared input contract: input.seed_registry: expected string, got integer'). If any of those refusals had disappeared, eligibility would have quietly absorbed execution safety. All of it ran in a scratch probe home that was removed afterwards.

ship_bar.item: run, eval-run, and forensic paths construct distinct caller contexts.
ship_bar.evidence: Three distinct flag sets, verified live. normal → allow_candidate:false, allow_retired:false, require_executed_provenance:true, require_current_ship:true. eval → true/false/false/false. forensic → true/true/false/false plus a required forensic_reason. The CLI refuses a forensic run with no reason: 'rcos: --purpose forensic requires --forensic <reason> — an override nobody can mistake for production reuse' (exit 2).

ship_bar.item: reuse_count, task text, semantic intent, scores and rankings cannot affect eligibility.
ship_bar.evidence: The caller-context vocabulary is closed at 8 keys (purpose, explicit_capability_id, allow_candidate, allow_retired, require_executed_provenance, require_current_ship, forensic_reason, scope). A 23-key forbidden vocabulary is refused rather than ignored: task_text → 'forbidden — eligibility may not see task text, semantic intent, scores, rankings or reuse history'; score → the same refusal. Unknown keys error too. The shape itself makes 'the payload cannot influence the decision' a property rather than a promise: a context carrying a task-like payload produces identical reasons to the same context carrying nothing.

ship_bar.item: Existing reuse and eval invariants remain unchanged.
ship_bar.evidence: Every stored reuse_count was cross-checked against T.deriveReuseCounts(T.loadTraces(HOME)): zero mismatches (the five legitimately non-zero counters are qr-camo-embed=4, hog-qa-suite=2, dell-gpu-dispatch=1, chalk-capture-recipe=1, muse-image-lane=1). reuse_count stays a cache of the trace log — never the registry certifying itself. The eval-mode dogfood invocation moved no counter: reuse-ledger's reuse_count is still 0.

canonical_reason_order.rule: Order the reasons by the order of the question each one answers: identity → permission → executability → evidence reality → evidence quality → context.
canonical_reason_order.why_this_rule: A reader of a decision should be able to stop at the first reason and know it is the most fundamental thing wrong, without the engine having to decide which reason 'matters most' — that would be a scoring judgment in a step that forbids scoring. Ordering by question-kind is structural, not preferential.
canonical_reason_order.executability_rule: Most specific first, and exactly ONE of these is ever emitted — they describe one underlying fact (this capability cannot be run here) at four levels of precision, so emitting several would report one problem as several.
canonical_reason_order.evidence_quality_rule: At most one is emitted: they are successive readings of the same evidence, not independent failures.
canonical_reason_order.rank_0_note: 'eligible' occupies rank 0 so the enumeration is total and a caller can compare ranks without special-casing success. It is guarded against ever appearing in a reasons array.

freshness.detail: eval_fresh is always the string 'unknown', and eval_stale can only fire from a runtime state that states staleness explicitly. No wall-clock comparison is made, because a freshness value nobody actually computed would be a fabrication inside a decision artifact — the one place the repo cannot afford one.
freshness.carried_forward: Freshness becomes a real axis when a later step defines what 'current' means for an eval. Until then the engine reports that it does not know.

decision_artifacts.integrity: semantic sha256 over JSON.stringify(document minus its integrity block, null, 2) + '\n' — deliberately NOT a byte hash, so reformatting is not treated as tampering while an edited verdict is
decision_artifacts.second_hash_layer: The byte-level pin travels separately, in the invocation manifest: eligibility_decision_id + eligibility_sha256 + an eligibility {scope, purpose, eligible, reasons, path} block, all re-hashed by verifyInvocation. Two layers, deliberately different: one asks 'is this document internally consistent', the other asks 'are these the exact bytes that authorised this run'.
decision_artifacts.note: The 9 written by the step-4 build are pinned in commit 187a61b. Four more were created by this receipt's own CLI dogfood (elig_20260918T032238Z-3d6a52, elig_20260918T032238Z-658e07, elig_20260918T032239Z-d78f78, elig_20260918T032307Z-4ab493) and were swept into commit 5a4d0f9 by the unrelated machine-written study loop before this receipt could pin them, because that loop stages everything it finds. They are disclosed here rather than hidden; all 13 verify clean. Decisions accumulate; they are never rewritten.

sweep.what: a read-only sweep that asks the eligibility engine about every capability in the real registry under every purpose; it calls evaluate(), which returns a decision without persisting one, so the sweep writes no registry byte, no trace byte and no decision artifact

behavior_changed: Permission and execution are now separate acts: the kernel cannot run anything without a decision artifact naming it.
A caller learns every applicable reason from one decision instead of one failure at a time.
Task text, semantic intent, scores, rankings and reuse history are refused at the context boundary rather than ignored inside the logic.
Forensic mode demands a written reason and cannot be entered silently.
Legacy capabilities now have a machine-readable name for why they cannot run in normal mode, instead of the repo merely knowing it in prose.
A decision is a durable, self-verifying artifact, so 'why did this run' is answerable from disk after the fact.
not_built_deliberately: any authority model, truth envelope or dependency graph
freshness computation (no clock is read; eval_fresh is 'unknown' by design)

verification_harness.note: One ship-bar check had to be corrected during receipt finalization, and it is disclosed here because a silently loosened check is worse than a failing one.
verification_harness.was: compared the live registry sha256 against a hardcoded step-4 value, which asserts that nothing has touched the registry since step 4. That is not what the ship bar asks and it is false in this repo, because an unrelated study loop commits on its own schedule; the check started failing for a reason that had nothing to do with this step.
verification_harness.now: checks the claim the ship bar actually makes, in two parts: the step-4 commit range bab54a7..187a61b must show an empty diff for registry/ and traces/, and any later divergence must be provably additive asserted eval records (same capability count, same id set, every non-evals field byte-identical, no eval removed, every added eval asserted). It fails on anything else.
verification_harness.result: PASS, with divergence_is_additive_evals_only true and an empty problems list
verification_harness.why_not_just_accept_it: loosening a check so it passes is the failure mode this whole step exists to prevent, so the check was made stricter in the direction that matters (it now inspects the content of the divergence, which the old one never did) rather than weaker.

not_done: No capability was made executable in this step. The 20 promoted legacy capabilities still declare no adapter, and no adapter was invented for them — that is a separate decision with its own evidence burden.
No selector, planner or ranking of any kind. The engine produces an eligible SET; choosing from that set is explicitly a later step and is explicitly not this one.
The compactor itself was not fixed. Its failing eval is now reported as a reason instead of being handled by prose.
Nothing was pushed. This repo has no remote; every commit in this chain is local only.
next_per_ruling: Step 4 ends at the eligibility engine. The boundary is now REGISTRY + EVAL STATE → ELIGIBILITY → eligible set → [future selector] → INVOCATION KERNEL, with the selector slot deliberately empty. Steps 5-13 remain unstarted and were not begun.
